text: Data Structures with Dr. Miller fit my evenings around long weeks at work, but the pacing dragged; I kept up with nearly every lecture, yet the dense weeks felt overwhelming and the instructions left too much interpretation, even as TAs answered promptly.

I’m a returning student kicking off this Data Structures course in my first semester, trying to juggle it with another heavy class, and I’m left with mixed impressions. The conceptual explanations are solid enough to ground the ideas, but the real-world examples feel thin, like we’re told what a binary search tree is without seeing how it actually behaves in a chunk of code I’ve tweaked myself. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and I’ve been to office hours once where a TA walked me through a bug I couldn’t shake on a small project, but I still walked away wondering how the assessments are supposed to map to what we’re told in lectures. The collaboration expectations feel murky; peers help each other more than staff does, and I’m not sure what count as a good group contribution for the weekly tasks. The mix of quizzes and a couple of bigger problem sets doesn’t line up with the lecture pace, and I’m left second-guessing whether I’m studying the right patterns for the exams. Overall, it’s not a total mess, but that mismatch sticks out, and I’m still rusty in spots I’d hoped would be clearer by now.

I took Computer Networks mainly to fit into my schedule, not out of some big interest in the topic, and that shaped how I approached it from day one. The material felt accessible at times, and the basic concepts were manageable, but the course still wore me out more than I expected—especially with the pace ramping up after each new topic. Dr. Chen’s delivery varies week to week; some lectures click and others feel like you’re chasing explanations, which made the weeks feel uneven. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which was a small relief when I was juggling other courses, but feedback came sparsely and often felt late, so I never quite knew where I stood before the next assignment. I found the course works best if you have a study group to bounce ideas off, since solo review of the lecture slides didn’t quite cut it. I earned a failing grade, yet I still have mixed feelings because some parts of the content were genuinely challenging in a way that stretched my understanding, even if the overall outcome was rough. Compared to another intro course I did this term, this one felt more exhausting but had some fair assessment moments that kept me pushing through. Overall, I’m not sure I’d recommend it, though I can see why someone else might find it doable with the right rhythm.

I’m new to the discipline and took Machine Learning mostly out of curiosity, and I’ll admit the course felt useful but not enjoyable. The explanations were solid on concepts, but the real-world examples never felt fleshed out enough to connect to what I’m seeing in labs or projects, so I spent most of the weeks relying on recordings and my own notes to pretend I understood how the pieces fit. The structure assumed more prior knowledge than I expected, and I kept thinking, “wait, do we really need that upstairs theorem for the homework?” The grading felt thorough in its comments, but the feedback arrived late enough that it didn’t help much for the next assignment, which was frustrating when time was ticking. I mostly worked alone, with a few small discussion threads that went nowhere; collaboration never clicked for me. My turning point came late in the semester during the final exam prep when I realized I could explain the high-level idea to a friend but couldn’t reproduce a concrete workflow for tuning a model without stumbling, which left me with a disappointing sense of what I actually learned. Overall, it’s a course I can see the value in, even if I didn’t enjoy it.

First semester in the program, and I’m glad I signed up for Cyber Security Basics because Prof. Cohen is clearly solid, approachable, and the lectures feel accessible even when the material is dense. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and the tool setup to actually run the labs took more effort than the payoff of getting hands-on practice, which was frustrating for someone trying to fit this around other commitments. I started the course fairly engaged, but as midterm tempo hit, attendance faded a bit and I found myself catching up from some sparse feedback that arrived after I already needed to move on. The course works a lot better if you have a study group, and I leaned on a couple classmates to decode the weekly tasks, which helped a lot when the pacing got wonky. Honestly, I learned a lot, but I also disliked the experience of battling the logistics more than the concepts, and I wish the feedback came sooner rather than after deadlines. If you don’t mind coordinating with others and tolerate a heavy setup, it’s worth sticking through.

I started off really engaged in Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez, and the organization of lectures and problem sets was solid, which helped since the LMS and submission flow are smooth. But the deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, so pacing felt rough and I found myself scrambling between topics, especially around the more advanced integrals. Still, the course fills prerequisite gaps better than I expected, and classmates often helped each other more than staff did, which kept us moving when I was uncertain about a concept like improper integrals.

I’m a returning student juggling a couple of demanding courses, and Operating Systems felt like it was testing my rusty basics more than anything else. Prof. Rios is clear in lectures, but the grading and the platform quirks created avoidable stress, especially when deadlines piled up and emails to support didn’t get quick answers. The course leaned heavy on reports and long writeups, not just quick problem sets, so I had to map out a week-by-week plan around the big deliverables. It helps that the class works better if you’ve got a study group; I leaned on a TA during office hours for one on one caveats about the project week, and I still remember a memorably tense second midterm week where the format felt like a surprise. Overall, it’s not a breeze, but the teaching style and the exam feel were fair enough.

Took Computer Networks with Prof. Cohen while working full-time, and my main takeaway is how the lectures feel solid on concepts but the concrete stuff never sticks—like the examples barely scratch the surface, so I left thinking, “okay, I get the why, not the how.” The assessments felt mismatched: quick-score quizzes peppered with code-reading questions, but the explanations behind the answers were thin, and the fast feedback rarely clarified where I went wrong, which didn’t help when deadlines piled up. I did appreciate the late-semester turning point around a networking lab, but the support channel, especially email, dragged when I needed guidance fast. Compared to the other course I took that term, this one left me tired and resigned rather than confident about applying anything to a real project.

Honestly, Cyber Security Basics was a mixed ride: I started off engaged, but my attendance faded as the semester dragged on and the workload piled up. I’m comfortable with proofs, not so much with system work, so the material felt a better fit once I leaned on the TAs and the forums to translate concepts into something usable. The project-heavy rhythm and high-stakes exams kept me honest, and the grading comments were thorough but came a bit late, which didn’t help when I was chasing feedback before a midterm. Office hours were a lifesaver, especially when I needed a quick sanity check on a threat model, and the instructor was solid, even if I didn’t always love the pace or the late rubric tweaks. Overall, it’s okay, and it helped for industry talk, but the practical parts pressed hard against my comfort zone.

Data Structures with Dr. Park started off the semester feeling pretty promising, but by mid‑semester my motivation slipped and so did my attendance, even though I had a decent amount of time—the workload and those platform quirks kept throwing me off more than I expected. The materials themselves felt scattered and often didn’t line up with what we were quizzed on, like the textbook section didn’t map cleanly to the weekly problem sets, which was frustrating when I just wanted a clear path through the stuff. The assessment design, on the other hand, finally clicked for me: the projects and the way the final design question tested real structure thinking made the whole thing feel worth it, even if the execution wasn’t smooth. I found the forums a mixed bag—some replies were genuinely helpful, others sounded dismissive and left me stuck for a bit longer than I wanted. I’m convinced the course works better if you hash things out in a study group, especially during the heavy crunch weeks, and I wish the instructions left a bit less room for interpretation. Still, there was a practical core to the material that felt useful, even if I didn’t enjoy every moment.

Taking Machine Learning in my first semester while juggling a full-time job felt like a sprint with a few long uphill stretches. Dr. Miller’s lectures were solid when I could attend, but the ramp-up quickly got dense, and the prerequisites started accessible and then slammed into real data work, which made catching up on evenings I had left besides work feel impossible at times. The forums helped, yet the responses sometimes sounded dismissive, like my basic questions were treated as off-topic noise, which wore on me. The assessment pattern leaned on heavy reports and time-consuming writeups, more than I expected, and the grading felt opaque—I’d hand in something I thought was clear and be unsure which parts blew the grade. I used the materials selectively—watching a few lectures here and there when a deadline loomed—so I didn’t build a steady study habit, and I ended up relying on one or two project elements rather than the full set of practicals. Compared to another course from the term, this one demanded more solo slog and had me thinking twice about taking it again, even though some code and a tool I learned did stick with me.

I just finished Linear Algebra this summer, and as a returning student I felt rusty enough that the pacing was a bit brutal but also oddly motivating. I kept up with nearly every lecture, partly because the peer discussion in our small groups helped more than the official Materials, and I’d find myself thinking through the proofs aloud with a classmate after the video timer paused. The lectures themselves are recorded and handy, but they can feel dry to sit through alone, so those quick in-between chats were the real anchor for me when I slipped on a concept I’d space on. The course moves through a lot for a compressed term, and the reports pile up in a way that makes you plan your week around the next deadline rather than the next concept, which I think suits the industry-use vibe I heard about beforehand—though the feedback comes fast, the explanations sometimes feel thin and I’m left to fill in a lot on my own. My standout memory is Week 6’s big matrix decomposition problem, which was intense in a way that stuck with me and kept me grading my own work against the professor’s notes; I wish the explanations around that topic had clicked sooner, but I guess that’s part of the ride.

I took Database Systems hoping it’d feel practical for industry work, but I left with mixed feelings and a rough mid-semester crunch that threw off my momentum. Dr. Chen is solid in lectures, yet the prerequisite feel like more than what was promised, and I found myself relying mostly on recordings and notes rather than live class energy. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, which helped during a tense week, but the assessments—a mix that didn’t line up well with what got covered in lectures—made it hard to feel confident about what mattered. I’d only recommend taking it if you’re prepared to put in extra prep and tolerate a bit of sloppy communication on administrative bits, plus don’t expect a tidy payoff.

Data Structures felt like a required step for my degree, and I kept pace with nearly every lecture because it mattered for my track. The course builds on the prerequisites pretty well, but the instructions sometimes left too much room for interpretation, which made the grading a bit of a moving target. I treated it as my main focus that term, juggling the heavy assignment workload with frequent deadlines, and the software stack started rough but became manageable after a couple of weeks. Compared to the other mid-program core course I took that term, this one was more practical but less enjoyable for me, and I’d only recommend it if you’ll come in prepared to wrangle the quirks and stay on top of every small deadline.

I took Operating Systems in my last semester before graduation mostly because I needed it for a specialization, and I’ll admit I dragged my feet on most of the theoretical stuff until the workload finally felt manageable. The pacing drove me a little crazy— lectures felt like they sprinted through topics I’d already skimmed but then hit a wall when I had to implement something real for the project, which didn’t help when I was juggling another hard class at the same time. The workload was honestly workable, but the administrative friction around tooling setup was frustrating: I spent an afternoon wrestling with a VM image and a weird permission issue that left me behind the first week. Dr. Chen is clearly knowledgeable, and the forums are helpful enough, though sometimes the responses came off as dismissive, which didn’t boost my motivation to ask questions. I mostly worked solo, with little peer dependency, and I found the assessment mix felt mismatched with what got lectured—like the exam brief didn't map cleanly to the weekly demos or the hands-on lab deliverables. One concrete gripe: the deadline pattern for the project felt arbitrary, and I ended up submitting in a rush after a long debugging session, which isn’t the best memory I want from my last machine-class course.

Cyber Security Basics was okay enough to get through mid‑semester chaos, especially since I was juggling a full-time job and a heavy load from another hard class. The course starts approachable but ramps up quickly, and I relied mostly on recordings and notes because live sessions felt long and a bit rushed. Tool setup took more effort than the payoff, and I felt the assessments matter a lot but come in a sparse rhythm—one memorable exam week sticks out, where the timing and format caught me by surprise. It works better with a study group, since collaboration fills gaps that the structure leaves a bit thin. All in all, not bad, just a lot of late nights and careful pacing.

Data Structures was a required slog this term, and the pacing felt off for me, especially juggling it with two other demanding courses. I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the workload for the week-long problem sets and the report-heavy midterm left me wondering if my grasp matched the grade; I liked the instructor, but the grading felt inconsistent and a bit arbitrary. The quick feedback helped enough to adjust, and the student help chats were more active than staff ones, which saved me on a few nights.

Overall, I’d say there’s a sense that this OS course is fine enough to finish, but the organization feels a bit messy for someone juggling a couple of other demanding classes in the final stretch before graduation. Prof. Haddad’s recorded lectures are handy when I’m rusty, but they’re pretty dry, and I end up rewatching sections just to catch a detail for a quiz that weighs heavily. The prerequisites hold up—what we build on makes sense—yet the collaboration expectations feel unclear, so I end up clarifying with teammates only after an awkward start. A single project about a small kernel module stands out, and it’s the most memorable bit, though the pace and cadence of deadlines in the term pattern weren’t helpful for planning. It’s usable, just not particularly smooth.

As a returning student juggling a full-time job, I kept up with nearly every lecture in Machine Learning this last semester before graduation, and I did notice the course had solid organization overall—schedules, deadlines, and a predictable rhythm helped me plan around the 8–10 page weekly report stuff. Yet the tooling kept throwing wrenches in, so deadlines felt longer than they should have, and the grading comments came with a lot of detail but arrived late enough to miss some fast-turnaround opportunities. Peer discussions were where the real clarity showed up for me, more than the official materials, and by the time the midterm project rolled around I found myself leaning on a concrete example I built for a previous role rather than the handouts. Overall, I don’t think I’d recommend it despite the value, but I’ll admit the structure kept things moving enough to finish.

Taking Computer Networks alongside a full-time job, I appreciated how the material felt practical even though I’m not a systems person. The TAs were quick and down-to-earth in the forums, like that office-hours chat where they helped me map a complex routing example to a real-world diag I was debugging at work. The grading felt off for the lectures sometimes, but I’ll keep the tricks I learned for the next project.

took Data Structures in the middle of a brutal semester, and i’m not sure i’d have survived without the recordings and notes, because the live sessions felt rushing and by the time i got to the second wave of topics i was already a bit lost. dr. singh explains things clearly enough and the pacing is decent on the lectures, but the workload and the steep ramp early on made every assignment feel like a trap that arrived right after a long class. the tooling setup took more effort than i expected for what we actually learned, and i spent more time fiddling with the environment than practicing actual data structures, which is frustrating because the payoff barely matched the effort. i’m new to the discipline, so the early examples helped, but the course ramps up fast and the prerequisite fit suddenly feels mismatched with what we’re asked to implement in the assessments. the mix of quizzes and a big final project didn’t align with the lectures in a lot of weeks, and i ended up relying on notes more than the live demos. overall, i can’t recommend it, even though i did pick up a few concrete concepts, and i’ll be glad when this term is done.

I took Data Structures during the summer term, and it started off with real engagement but then my attendance faded as the pace got compressed and the workload piled up. I actually found the peer discussions helpful—my study group kept me afloat when the official materials felt like a slog—though the reporting-heavy tasks dragged on, easily eating up evenings. The tooling was decent, and the prerequisites fit my gaps better than I expected, which surprised me in a good way. Admin feedback arrived too late to influence my approach, and by the end I was tired and resigned, with mixed feelings about how much I learned versus how rough the experience was.

This last semester in Database Systems felt uneven: I learned a lot from the peer discussions but hated the platform quirks that added avoidable stress, and I kept using the materials only when needed. The project with SQL queries and the midterm felt mismatched to lectures, yet feedback came quickly enough to adjust.

This course kept me curious about databases, but the grading felt vague and the rubric always seemed to shift last minute, which didn’t help when deadlines piled up. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, and the tool glitches during week-long deadlines made everything feel downhill, especially since email support dragged its feet. I wouldn’t take it again, even though the material helped me on a later project about indexing, and I’d compare it unfavorably to the other course from this term.

I’m new to linear algebra, and the slides are serviceable but not memorable, so I relied on the projects to feel the concepts. I kept up late around deadlines while juggling work, and the grading felt high-stakes but fair enough.

Dr. Singh’s Machine Learning class was heavy on concepts, but the concrete examples were thin, and feedback often arrived too late to help. I fell behind and only caught up near deadlines; the first-semester prep felt like it expects adjacent material I hadn’t mastered.

Data Structures was okay to fill a prerequisite for a specialization, but the support felt thin and the grading transparency was rough. I relied mostly on recordings, and the quick feedback helped adjust, though the project-heavy setup stressed me out. Office hours helped once.

I’m coming off the summer term with a stronger than expected coding baseline but really underwhelmed by how the theory stuff was handed to us in Machine Learning with Dr. Miller. The pacing felt frantic, and I ran into tooling hiccups during deadline weeks that made a couple of modules drag on longer than they should have, which didn’t help when I was juggling two other demanding courses. I remember an early confusion about the difference between bias-variance and regularization cropping up in week two, which then colored how I read the later problem sets and kinda stuck with me through the term. The collaboration expectations felt murky too; we were told to “coordinate more,” but the rubric and the workspace rules didn’t line up, so some partners seemed to do the heavy lifting while others just hung back. Grading rubrics were vague enough that it was hard to know what counted for partial credit on the final project, and that ambiguity lingered longer than I’d like. On the bright side, the organization around lecture slides and office hours sometimes paid off, and the in-person sessions could be solid when the day’s topic clicked, especially when we hit a practical example with a quick code walkthrough.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester, and this Database Systems course has felt like a steady grind with a few bright spots. I started out fairly engaged, but as the weeks piled up I slipped into shorter evening study sessions and it’s been hard to keep the momentum going, especially since the tool setup to run the lab workflows took more effort than I expected for the payoff. The feedback is detailed when it finally lands, but I’m often waiting a week or more to see comments on assignments, which makes it hard to adjust quickly. One concrete thing I’ll remember: the midterm had a tricky query optimization prompt that required more prior intuition than the lectures emphasized, and that mismatch lingered.

Calculus II in the summer term dragged along with a compressed pace, and I kept up with nearly every lecture while trying to fit short evening study sessions around work. The lectures were clear and moved at a decent clip, but the relevance of some topics felt off for how I actually use calculus later, especially compared to the previous prerequisite course, which felt easier and more directly applicable. Assessments were few but felt weighty, and I’m still unsure if my C reflected real understanding or just a rough mid-semester crunch. Most of the help I got happened among peers; staff-backed support was thinner, and I remember noodling through an assignment line-by-line in the forum after hours with a classmate, which saved us more than once. Overall, I’m not sure I’d recommend it outright.

I took Computer Networks mainly out of curiosity, but the class veered into a lot of walls of text and dense theory that felt unnecessarily hard for an advanced elective. Grading comments are solid when they arrive, but feedback arrives late, and the platform quirks caused avoidable stress during a mid-semester crunch. I took Linear Algebra kind of hoping it would pay off for industry work, and the summer term sprint felt extra brutal with the pace. The instructor was engaging, but the grading felt inconsistent, which left me second-guessing whether the project heavy load was about mastery or ticking boxes. The LMS flow was smooth and the recorded lectures helped on long nights, though some equations in the videos felt dry and forgettable. My turning point was near the end when a late-project realization clicked, but overall I’m solid B and felt it matched the effort.

I’d say my experience with Operating Systems this summer was mostly lukewarm, honest but not exactly smooth. The pacing felt really compressed for a summer term, and Dr. Park’s delivery seemed uneven week to week, which didn’t help when I was juggling motivation that wandered between “I can stay on track” and “I’ll just cram later.” The workload is heavily project-heavy with high-stakes exams, and the tooling setup was a constant friction point that stalled me for days—think tangled virtual environments and a few flaky scripts. In discussions and office hours, I saw peers helping each other more than staff did, and I found myself wishing for a bit more straightforward guidance, especially around the forum threads where the answers sometimes arrive after deadlines.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and this Cyber Security Basics class kept me on my toes despite a rough week-to-week pace from Prof. Alvarez. The forums helped, but the grading comments arrived late and I sometimes hit the curve—still, the organization kept me marginally afloat.

Calculus II with Dr. Park was a slog from the moment I started it last semester, strapped to a full-time job and another hard class, and it showed most when the deadlines hit during weeks with tooling glitches that would randomly crash our submission portal. I began the term engaged, showing up to the first few lectures and using office hours to wrestle through parametric integrals, but my attendance faded mid‑semester as the workload and the time crunch kept piling up. The course felt project-heavy with high-stakes exams, and even when the assessments felt fair, they left me exhausted by the end of the week; the feedback arrived sparsely until it was basically too late to act on it for the next deadline. The admin side was okay in theory—policies loosened enough to juggle the big assignments—but communication was sloppy, so I spent more time chasing clarifications than actually solving problems. I remember a particular week where the project dashboard showed a new rubric at the last minute, and I had to scramble with a ta and the TA's forum thread to confirm what counted toward the final grade. It’s not all bad, but the combination of continuous time pressure and inconsistent tooling made the course feel like a marathon I was barely funded for.

I barely passed Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Haddad, because the lectures were useful but dry and I only used the materials when needed; the project-heavy setup and vague grading rubric left me unsure, though TAs were responsive and I managed the deadlines okay.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Cyber Security Basics, but I felt overwhelmed by the prerequisite fit and found the tooling hard to navigate; the fast feedback helps but leaves explanations thin, and the one big project mattered a lot more than I expected.

took intro computer networks with prof. haddad while juggling a full-time job, so I relied on the recorded lectures—they help but feel dry and a bit overlong. early on I mixed up a subnet calc and it stuck with me, shaping the term oddly.

Data Structures in my first semester was… honestly rough, but in a useful way. The tool setup felt like a chores list that never ends, and the ramp from accessible to tough hit me hard—by week four I was already thinking about dropping, yet I still see how it connects to industry work, sometimes. I’m a returning student who felt a bit rusty, but the Linear Algebra course under Dr. Miller kept a steady pace and leaned on clear lectures, which helped me get back into the material without panic. The workload felt positive overall, with a handful of big assessments where each one actually matters—so you stay on top rather than sprinting. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, since attendance was flexible, and I appreciated that the practical work lined up with what we’d cover in class, from matrix decompositions to real-world data vibes. One quirk I noticed was the grading rubric, which felt a bit vague, and by the end I wished for a tighter sense of how partial credit mapped to the final score. Still, I’d recommend the course broadly, especially if you’re catching up after a pause.

I’m comfortable with proofs but not systems work, and this course felt like it started accessible and then ramped up hard, which left me juggling concepts I didn’t expect to chase in the middle of a semester. The thing that stuck with me is how the feedback kept arriving late and sparse, so when I finally got a grading nudge, I’d already moved on to the next module and wasn’t in the frame of mind to adjust. The collaboration expectations were unclear, so I ended up working mostly solo even though the project-heavy setup suggested team input would help, and I didn’t feel the rubric actually aligned with the big exams at the end. I appreciated the instructor—clear explanations during lectures—but the grading felt inconsistent, as if different TAs weighed the same work differently, which was demotivating. Tooling was another drag: the network emulator we were told to rely on was finicky, and the interface didn’t play nicely with my usual workflow. Compared to the easier prerequisite, this one hits you with more proofs and fewer guardrails, and I can’t say I’d recommend it, though I did pick up a few useful ideas I’ll carry into the track.

Database Systems felt rusty and haphazard; the slides were serviceable but not memorable, and the prerequisites ramped up fast enough to leave me flustered when I started the week 3 labs. I used the materials selectively, and that uneven motivation showed up in my C.

I stuck with nearly every lecture out of genuine curiosity, but the course felt bogged down by how the tooling and setup kept biting into deadlines, which made the weeks feel heavier than they should. The slides were serviceable, but I left with mixed feelings after a midterm crunch that somehow amplified the impression that the menu of assignments was the main driver, not the learning. I remember the first big confusion about process scheduling and how it colored the rest of the term.

Calculus II fit the bill as a required starter for the program, and I focused on it as my main course that term. The lecturer’s explanations clicked on concepts, but the examples felt thin, and the platform quirks added a bit of stress during homework submissions. I appreciated that the course filled gaps in prerequisites better than I expected, and I remember one forum reply during office hours clarifying a tricky integration step, which kept me calmer than I expected to be.

Taking Machine Learning with Dr. Chen last semester was a mixed ride, especially since I’m a returning student trying to shake off rust and fit study around short evening sessions. The course material felt relevant and leaned into real projects, but the big thing that stuck was how unpredictable the feedback was: some assignments came back quickly with concrete pointers, others slid in late and felt like they’d been judged with a different rubric than I expected. The workload was very assignment-heavy, with frequent deadlines, and I felt the crunch during mid-semester when balancing a rough calendar and the light touch of the official handouts didn’t quite line up. I found peer discussions more helpful than the official slides or reading, which weirdly made the collaboration structure feel secondary to what classmates said in the hall after class. One concrete memory: the final project required a barebones model in Python, plus a short write-up, and the grading quirk about whether the narrative matched the code felt arbitrary and left me scrambling to align both parts at the last minute. Overall, the fit for my late-stage, rusty-self approach was decent, even with the timing quirks and the uneven feedback.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Cyber Security Basics, but the pace and heavy assignments left me wishing for clearer theory links; that early confusion about why certain controls mattered shaped the rest of the term, and the tool setup was a slog every week.

Data Structures was an early warning bell I didn’t want to hear: the workload felt endless for an advanced elective, and I made it the main focus of my term, which wasn’t the best idea. I liked Prof. Alvarez and the way he explained concepts in the recorded lectures, but they were consistently dry to sit through, especially when the recordings dragged on and on with code snapshots that didn’t always click for me. The grading was the bigger mess—a lot of the feedback felt inconsistent week to week, and I’m unsure whether the C I ended with actually reflected my understanding, especially after one late-semester project that felt rushed and oddly counted against me. Most work was solo, with little peer dependency, which left me spinning on some problems and craving a quicker email ping from support when deadlines loomed, because the email replies were slow and I’d miss a sub-deadline. There was one turning point around the second-to-last assignment where I finally felt I understood how the graphs module should behave, but that moment was muddied by the grading quirks and the feeling that the course didn’t reward the right kind of effort. Overall, I’d only recommend with serious preparation and a tolerance for rough feedback cycles.

Taking Data Structures in my last semester, I picked it mostly to fit the schedule with my other demanding courses, not because I’m obsessed with the topic. The group work helped when the team actually coordinated, but I felt the tooling and platform hiccups dragged weeks late on each deadline, which piled up my stress. The instruction felt uneven week to week, and the grading comments were detailed but showed up after the due date, which didn’t help me adjust in time. It’s an advanced elective, so prereqs felt borderline; I’m glad I stuck with it, and I’d still recommend it to others who can juggle a few late nights. For me, the project with the memory map and the toolchain quirk stands out more than the lectures.

I liked Dr. Park, but the assignment-heavy pace and fast feedback felt thin and a bit cold, especially during a mid‑semester crunch. The tooling setup was a slog, and I mainly relied on recordings; it’s hard to call the grading fair when explanations are sparse.

I’m comfortable with proofs, but Linear Algebra mostly felt like a slog through the same ideas, and I’m unsure it really showed I understood the material. Prof. Alvarez answered questions quickly in office hours and the LMS flow was smooth, but collaboration expectations were unclear and I often wondered what counted as a gram of effort for the group work. Calculus II sat in the middle of a brutal semester, and I felt like I was riding a roller coaster between my strong coding chops and the shaky theory stuff the course kept throwing at us. The software stack started rough—compiled plots failing, random MathJax hiccups in the notes, and a few tools that felt half-broken until I hacked my own workaround—but it eventually became usable enough to get by. The assessment setup was deliberate: only a handful of tasks, but each one actually counted a lot toward the final grade, which meant I treated every quiz and problem set like a make-or-break checkpoint. The feedback I got came back fast, but the explanations were pretty thin, like a quick line of “good job” with little rationale or pointers for what to fix next, which left me guessing how to improve. Given my background in coding and weak exposure to the underlying theory, I found the proofs and the abstraction-heavy parts harder to anchor, especially around the middle of the term when fatigue set in and I finally realized I needed a more solid theoretical anchor. If I compare it to the prerequisite, this felt easier in some procedural sense but less forgiving in the jump to real analysis, and I’m not sure I’d take it again even though I did pull a solid B that matched the effort I put in. A turning point came late when I finally connected the differential equation techniques back to the column of notes I’d been treating as separate modules, and that little insight kept me grounded through the last few weeks.
